summary.text: At \(n=140\), rational bounds on \(\sqrt5\) give the exact values \(a(140)=471\), \(a(144)=484\), \(a(157)=528\), and \(a(161)=542\). The proposed relation would instead require \(a(161)=528+484-471=541\), contradicting \(a(161)=542\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor,
\qquad n\ge 1.
\]
We disprove the proposed identity
\[
a(n+21)=a(n+17)+a(n+4)-a(n)
\]
by evaluating it at the single admissible value \(n=140\).

Put
\[
\alpha=\sqrt{\frac54}.
\]
Since \(\alpha\ge 0\) and \(\alpha^2=5/4\), for every positive integer \(m\), if \(x=m\alpha\), then
\[
(2x)^2=4m^2\alpha^2=5m^2.
\]
Thus, to prove \(\lfloor m\alpha\rfloor=k\), it suffices to prove
\[
(2k)^2\le 5m^2<\bigl(2(k+1)\bigr)^2.
\]
Indeed, all quantities involved are nonnegative, so these inequalities between squares imply
\[
2k\le 2m\alpha<2(k+1),
\]
and hence
\[
k\le m\alpha<k+1.
\]
This is exactly the condition that \(\lfloor m\alpha\rfloor=k\).

We now carry this out for the four indices occurring when \(n=140\).

First, for \(m=140\) and \(k=156\),
\[
(2\cdot156)^2=312^2=97344,
\]
\[
5\cdot140^2=5\cdot19600=98000,
\]
and
\[
(2\cdot157)^2=314^2=98596.
\]
Therefore
\[
97344\le 98000<98596,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). Consequently,
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

Second, for \(m=144\) and \(k=160\),
\[
(2\cdot160)^2=320^2=102400,
\]
\[
5\cdot144^2=5\cdot20736=103680,
\]
and
\[
(2\cdot161)^2=322^2=103684.
\]
Hence
\[
102400\le 103680<103684,
\]
which gives
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Since \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), we obtain
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

Third, for \(m=157\) and \(k=175\),
\[
(2\cdot175)^2=350^2=122500,
\]
\[
5\cdot157^2=5\cdot24649=123245,
\]
and
\[
(2\cdot176)^2=352^2=123904.
\]
Thus
\[
122500\le 123245<123904,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Moreover, \(157=4\cdot39+1\), and therefore \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\). It follows that
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

Finally, for \(m=161\) and \(k=180\),
\[
(2\cdot180)^2=360^2=129600,
\]
\[
5\cdot161^2=5\cdot25921=129605,
\]
and
\[
(2\cdot181)^2=362^2=131044.
\]
Therefore
\[
129600\le129605<131044,
\]
and hence
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
As \(161=4\cdot40+1\), we also have \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Consequently,
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

Now specialize the conjectured recurrence to \(n=140\). Since
\[
140+21=161,\qquad 140+17=157,\qquad 140+4=144,
\]
it would assert
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
But the exact values found above give
\[
a(157)+a(144)-a(140)=528+484-471=541,
\]
whereas
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus the proposed equality at \(n=140\) would be \(542=541\), which is false. Since \(140\ge1\), this is a valid counterexample to the universal claim. Therefore the conjectured recurrence does not hold for every \(n\ge1\).
